visible.summary:
Louisiana posts the country's highest measured killing rate against trans women: 24.7 per 100k trans women per year reported, 11.6 recorded, on the TGEU trans-murder-monitoring base (428 US victims, 2008–2025) — a floor rather than a total, though the same analysis cautions that legal-risk rankings do not sort physical safety, and the top-ranked state records 23.5. In custody, a 45-year-old Black trans woman serving a life sentence was killed by other inmates at Angola prison on 2 April 2024, at least the 16th violent death of a trans or gender-expansive person that year; killings continued into 2026.

On 31 May 2026 a mob of about ten beat a trans couple, Aurora Rush and Shae Sanders, outside a women's restroom at a park in Benton; no attacker was arrested, while both victims were charged with disturbing the peace and Rush was jailed in a men's facility and searched by a male guard despite a female marker on her licence. On 15 July 2026 the Bossier Parish Police Jury unanimously approved — on the first of two required votes, reportedly at the sheriff's request — a local ordinance criminalising trans restroom use, described as one of the most punitive in the country. Louisiana has no statewide adult bathroom ban, so the parish ordinance is the state's sharpest instrument.
visible.tangentialFactors: Statewide K-12/facility ban (2024) and a state binary-'sex' definition law (2026) set the legal frame that emboldened the parish ordinance and the 'protecting the children' framing of the mob (dossier; MAP equality map).

sources.claim: The Needle national analysis (July 2026, TGEU/Williams data): Louisiana records the highest per-capita killing rate of trans women of any state — 24.7 per 100k per year reported (19 recorded) against the top 'safest' state's 23.5 — on a base of 428 US victims 2008–2025; every figure is an undercount floor, and the piece cautions legal-risk rankings do not sort physical safety, with the worst-law states holding the highest rate.

Metro Weekly (Aug 2026): a mob beat trans couple Aurora Rush and Shae Sanders over restroom use at Cypress Black Bayou Park, Benton; Sanders (pre-existing spinal injury) and Rush (concussion, blood pooling) were both charged with disturbing the peace while no attacker was arrested; Rush was jailed in a men's facility and searched by a male guard despite a 'female' marker on her driver's licence.

Erin in the Morning (5 Aug 2026): the same Benton mob attack — victims charged rather than their attackers, plea deal not signed; reports the municipality simultaneously voted one of the country's most severe anti-trans restroom ordinances; Rush was denied hospital care and taken to a men's jail, and no one else was arrested that day per the Sheriff's Office.

HRC memorial (11 June 2024): Yella (Robert) Clark Jr., a 45-year-old Black trans woman serving a life sentence at Angola prison, was killed in a fight with several inmates on 2 April 2024 — at least the 16th trans or gender-expansive person HRC had learned of killed in 2024 and the fifth in April alone, with such deaths systematically under- or mis-reported.

visible.summary:
Texas operates one of the country's most actively enforced anti-trans regimes. Its facilities law (the SB 8 'Women's Privacy Act', in force 4 December 2025) produced enforcement within days: state troopers checked identification at women's restrooms in the Capitol while cities and campuses adopted sharply divergent compliance and evasion policies, and the attorney general opened the first state bathroom-law enforcement inquiry of its kind — against an Austin school district, escalated with a second records demand in April 2026 after a tip-line complaint.

Violence exposure is the national worst in absolute terms: 44 recorded killings of trans women over 2008–2025 (about 7.6 per 100k trans women per year; the monitoring project frames all rates as undercount floors). A July 2026 law-by-law legal-risk assessment grades Texas in its top 'Do Not Travel' tier.
visible.tangentialFactors: LGB-facing visibility is rolling back too: Arlington's city council rescinded its LGBTQ non-discrimination ordinance (Dec 2025) and Arlington Pride suspended its 2026 events; a Houston-area venue pulled out of Katy Pride under school-board pressure.
visible.localsOnly: Document governance is resident-facing but nationally anomalous: DPS has ignored court-ordered gender-marker changes and built a database of applicants seeking them.

sources.claim: Texas Tribune (12 Dec 2025): SB 8 implementation — DPS troopers ID-checked people at women's restrooms outside the Capitol on 6 Dec 2025 (trans women holding female ID markers were admitted), the Austin City Council moved to circumvent the law's intent, and opponents warn unclear guidelines produce uneven, invasive enforcement; protests followed at the Capitol.

Austin Current (27 Apr 2026): Attorney General Paxton's second complaint escalated the state probe of Austin ISD over bathroom policy, with a renewed records demand after a tip-line complaint — the first state bathroom-law enforcement inquiry against a school district.

The Needle national analysis (July 2026, TGEU/Williams data): Texas carries the highest absolute toll of any state — 44 recorded killings of trans women 2008–2025, about 7.6 per 100k per year (undercount floor) — within the map's 'Do Not Travel' grading.

Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map, July 2026 update: Texas is one of four states in the top 'Do Not Travel' tier for adult trans travellers (with Florida, Idaho and Kansas), graded law-by-law across care bans, bathroom bans and enforcement posture by a five-year legislation-tracking methodology.

visible.summary:
Utah's HB 257 (January 2024) was the first statewide bathroom ban in the country reaching trans adults, not only school facilities; it remains in force, alongside birth-certificate and surgery requirements for amended markers and a complaint channel for objecting officials.

In May 2025 Utah became the first state to explicitly prohibit flying LGBTQ flags at government buildings and schools (fines up to $500 per day), with similar flag bans following in other states — its Pride organisation calls the state's legislative record the nation's most anti-LGBT.
visible.tangentialFactors: The flag ban and the 2025 Pride-season sponsor exodus are visibility conflicts affecting LGBT+ presence broadly rather than trans status specifically - but they shape the climate a visibly trans visitor encounters, and enforcement of the $500/day flag fines reaches ordinary institutional spaces.

sources.claim: Guardian report (29 May 2025) on Pride 2025 in the US: on 7 May Utah became the first state to explicitly prohibit flying LGBTQ+ flags at government buildings and schools, with fines of $500 a day; Utah Pride's executive director says the state 'leads the nation in anti-LGBTQ legislation'; similar flag bans were signed in Idaho and Montana, while Salt Lake City issued counter-flags and Boise made the pride flag an official city flag.

On Jan. 30, 2024, Republican Gov. Spencer Cox signed HB 257, making Utah the latest state to regulate bathroom access for transgender people; the law requires people to use bathrooms and locker rooms in public schools and government-owned buildings that match their sex assigned at birth. Under the legislation transgender people can defend themselves against complaints by showing documentation of gender-affirming care, and new government buildings must include single-occupant bathrooms. NBC reported at least 10 other states had passed similar bathroom-regulation laws by then and quoted the ACLU of Utah opposing the bill for risking discriminatory enforcement. This is the dated enactment of the adult-reaching bathroom ban the record attributes to HB 257.

Official Utah Legislature page for HB 257 ('Sex-based Designations for Privacy, Anti-bullying, and Women's Opportunities'): the bill's action history shows it was introduced Jan. 11, 2024, advanced through House and Senate committee and floor stages across several substitute versions, and the page's last recorded action is '30 Jan 2024, Governor Signed.' Subject tags cover state facilities, K-12 and higher education, and health and human services. Primary state-government confirmation of the bill number, short title and Jan. 30, 2024 signing date.

Star Observer documents the reporting mechanism Utah set up under HB 257: a form through which residents can report transgender people in 'privacy spaces' such as changing rooms and restrooms, with complainants able to choose whether their names are included while the state investigates each 'violation'. The article says the form implements HB 257, 'Sex-Based Designations for Privacy, Anti-Bullying and Women's Opportunities', passed in January 2024, which banned trans Utahns from using bathrooms or competing in a sport that matches their gender identity. This confirms the complaint channel the record lists among Utah's facility-law provisions.

visible.summary:
Florida's 2023 law (Fla. Stat. 553.865) makes it a second-degree criminal trespass — up to 60 days — to remain in a public bathroom or changing facility that does not match sex assigned at birth after a government employee orders departure; the ACLU of Florida calls it 'complex, confusing, and vague' and of limited actual coverage, and among at least 14 states with facility restrictions only Florida and Utah criminalise the act itself.

In March 2025 a 20-year-old trans student was arrested using a women's restroom in the State Capitol — believed the first arrest anywhere under a state bathroom ban. A Leon County judge dismissed the charge in June 2025 on speedy-trial grounds after the state missed a 90-day filing deadline; because the arrest was booked as trespass, the ban's constitutionality was never reached. Equality Florida and the Human Rights Campaign have issued named travel advisories warning of risks to trans travellers and movers.

Physical safety is comparatively better than the law suggests: a July 2026 analysis puts Florida's recorded killing rate for trans women at 3.7 per 100k per year, below the average of the worst-law states — itself an undercount floor.
visible.tangentialFactors: Pride and civic visibility are being rolled back statewide — removal of Pride crosswalks, with Orlando residents defying the state — visibility conflicts affecting LGBT+ presence broadly rather than trans status specifically.
visible.outOfScopeNotes: The travel advisory itself also cites non-trans laws (reproductive-health restrictions, gun-safety repeals, curriculum censorship); those shape the general rights climate but do not move trans-specific visitor risk.

sources.claim: ACLU Florida know-your-rights on the 2023 restroom law (Fla. Stat. 553.865): refusing to leave a sex-segregated restroom or changing facility can be criminal trespass, but the law only applies in buildings owned or leased by the state or local government — state offices, courthouses, legislative offices, prisons/jails, local immigration detention, state parks and toll-road plazas — and purports to cover all schools, public or private. Private businesses are outside its scope; the ACLU advises fact-specific judgment and legal counsel.

NBC News (2025): Marcy Rheintgen, a 20-year-old trans college student, was arrested at the Florida State Capitol after declaring 'I am here to break the law' and entering a women's restroom — believed to be the first arrest under Florida's transgender bathroom restrictions. She faces a misdemeanor trespass charge punishable by up to 60 days in jail; at least 14 states have adopted laws barring trans women from women's bathrooms at schools and some government buildings.

Metro Weekly (July 6, 2025): on June 20, 2025 Leon County Judge Lashawn Riggans threw out the trespass case against Marcy Rheintgen on a legal technicality — as a defendant charged under the Safety in Private Spaces Act she had no standing to argue the law itself was illegitimate — so the statute was never substantively tested. She had been charged March 19, 2025 after police, alerted in advance, arrested her washing her hands in a women's restroom at the Statehouse.

Equality Florida travel advisory (April 12, 2023): the organization took the 'unprecedented step' of warning about risks to the health, safety and freedom of those considering short or long-term travel or relocation to Florida, citing laws hostile to LGBTQ people, reproductive-health restrictions, gun-safety rollbacks, and book bans/curriculum censorship. The advisory followed a wave of visitor safety inquiries; EQFL reports events and conferences cancelling and notes the US military considering redeployment for service members' families.

National law-vs-violence analysis (2008-2025 data): Florida scores 8.0 on the anti-trans law scale with 3.7 trans women murdered per 100k per year, labelled 'Do Not Travel'; the article's core finding is that state law severity does not correlate with killing rates (trendline nearly flat across the 26 states with data) — legal climate and street-level violence are independent visitor risks.

visible.summary:
Montana has passed laws that would grade among the country's worst — including a facility-use ban and a public-buildings bathroom ban — but state courts have repeatedly blocked or enjoined them under the state constitution, leaving little of the anti-trans statutory book in force.

That makes Montana the anomaly of the 2026 legal-risk assessments: the only state whose risk grade was lowered — from 'worst laws' to 'high risk' — by cumulative court rulings and injunctions, in the February 2026 cycle. Statutory risk is high; enforcement risk is genuinely mixed.
visible.tangentialFactors: The pride-flag ban reaches symbols displayed on public buildings rather than trans people's conduct, facilities or documents — an ideological-climate signal for visitors rather than a direct mechanism.

sources.claim: July 2026 anti-trans national risk assessment: Montana is flagged as a special case — it has passed laws that would normally place it among the worst states, but those laws have been repeatedly blocked or enjoined under the state constitution, improving its standing on the assessment's rubric (which ranks states by expert reading of bills on adult and youth restrictions).

National risk assessment update: Montana is the single state that improves in the 2026 rankings, because the state court system has repeatedly blocked or enjoined anti-trans laws under the state constitution; adult restrictions that were passed have not taken full effect. Youth-side picture remains unstable nationally (federal policy shifts and litigation).

visible.summary: Highest per-capita incident load in the country: 72 recorded anti-LGBTQ incidents in 2025 in a state of ~1.4m. Counterweight: in July 2026 a county court found an attacker violated the NH Civil Rights Act after striking a trans gas-station employee, using his pronoun refusal as bias evidence, with bodycam showing officers correcting his pronoun use — institutions working. Slightly below the national score 0.36.
visible.tangentialFactors: Anti-trans campaigners took legal action against a small school district over a trans athlete — local climate pressure rather than a statewide rule, but part of the same visibility conflict.

sources.claim: GLAAD 2025 national incident census: New Hampshire recorded 72 anti-LGBTQ incidents in 2025 — second-highest of any state after California (198), ahead of Texas (66), Ohio (50) and Washington (50).

Concord Monitor/NHPR (17 Jul 2026): Merrimack County Superior Court found a Concord man violated the New Hampshire Civil Rights Act by striking a transgender woman; republished by NHPR with the Granite State News Collaborative.
